text: Good morning, may it please the court. This is Bobby Palmer for the appellee department. Appellate department. Deputies ultimately were able to block Aiden's vehicle with their vehicles, but Aiden attempted to break away from the deputies' vehicles by ramming his vehicle forward and in reverse, thereby spinning and smoking his tires, all the while ignoring commands to stop and ignoring commands to put up his hands. Deputies pleaded for Aiden to raise his hands, but he did not. Instead, he dropped his right hand to his waistband, resulting in deputies firing at him for fear he was reaching for a weapon. At no time did any of the deputies observe Aiden raise his hands in order to surrender before he was shot. We're here today on an appeal by the appellant relating to two post-trial motions filed with the trial court. One was the motion to interview the juror, and the other was the motion for new trial because of alleged juror misconduct. The appellant's two post-trial motions both related to the alleged juror misconduct on the part of a juror named Joan Fortin and her alleged failure to provide information to Dr. Fordyre about her alleged involvement in three county court cases, which took place in 2007, 2009, and 2014, regarding the collection of credit card debt. Ultimately, the court entered an order on each of those post-trial motions, denying them, and one of the reasons why it was denied is because they were unsworn. Portions of the trial transcript, which would address the three additional issues raised for the first time on appeal, are not part of the record. With regard to the motion to interview juror of, especially with Joan Fortin, it is important to note that when the Florida Supreme Court decided Baptist Hospital of Miami versus Mala, it stated in no uncertain terms that an inquiry regarding interviewing a juror is never permissible unless the moving party has sworn the allegations. I think it's very significant that the Florida Supreme Court has said never permissible. So at the very outset, appellant's motion for interview of the juror was defective on its face for not complying with the minimum requirement mandated by the Florida Supreme Court, that is, that it be sworn. Furthermore, this case, excuse me, this court, when Travelers Insurance Company versus Jackson in 1992 held in a case where not only was the motion for new trial not sworn, but the motion to interview jurors was not sworn, in that case, this court reiterated Baptist Hospital's mandate. And in this case, not only was the motion to interview juror not sworn, but the motion for new trial was not sworn either. So the trial court, in fact, in its orders, denying the motion to interview juror and the motion for new trial, cited as the very first reason for denial is that neither of the motions were sworn. The court is mindful that when we're talking about interviewing a juror, the Florida Supreme Court has given us guidelines in the De La Rosa case decided in 1995. In that De La Rosa case, there are three prongs that must be satisfied before a motion to interview juror is, in fact, to be granted. Now, that's assuming, of course, that it's sworn to begin with, which was not the case in the case so far. So the greater weight of Florida jurisprudence holds that post-trial juror interviews are to be rarely granted. And the sanctity of the jury process, as well as the privacy rights of the jurors themselves, should be closely guarded and protected. And post-trial jury interviews are disfavored by the courts and are only allowed in very rare circumstances. And this is certainly not one of them. The first prong of the De La Rosa case was not met by the planning. The first prong relates to whether or not the information is relevant and material. And in the first prong of this, the court considered all the arguments made by the parties, as well as the written arguments. And Appelli's arguments were the same then as they are now. The court, in fact, considered all of that, considered all the case law. And the trial court did not abuse its discretion in finding that the first prong of De La Rosa analysis was not met because the undisclosed information not only must be relevant, but it must also be material to the jury service in the case. We know that from the Roberts case decided by the Florida Supreme Court in 2002. De La Rosa did not dictate that all prior litigation history is per se material. And the test is not whether the information is relevant and material in general, but whether it is relevant material to the jury service in this case. And materiality must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis. We know from the Roberts case that the decision as to whether a juror's involvement in a particular prior legal matter is material should be primarily made at the trial level because materiality is fact-intensive. It is there that the dynamics and the context of the entire trial process can be evaluated by the trial court. In this particular case, we must also remember that the Florida Supreme Court has told us that whether a particular prior litigation by a juror is material and relevant is also the subject of whether it is remote in time. And all of these prior cases allegedly involving this juror were all remote in time. And I've cited in Apelli's answer brief cases where prior litigation history was, in fact, deemed to be too remote in time to be material. And so the second prong of the De La Rosa analysis was not met either. Ms. Fortin answered every single question directly when she was asked the direct question. And there was no reason to believe that when she asked direct questions, she concealed anything. The third prong of the De La Rosa analysis was also not met. And I have cited case law from the Third District Court of Appeal in 2013, where it was determined that an appellant's post-trial motion to interview a juror based upon post-trial research, which was something that could have been publicly and easily available at the time of the trial, was not obtained by the appellant until after an adverse verdict was received. Therefore, I believe, like in that case, as well as in this case, the third prong of the De La Rosa analysis was not, in fact, met because of a lack of diligence on the part of the appellant at the trial. In concluding, the trial court correctly ruled on the cause challenge of Juror Austin, correctly ruled on the appellant's objection to appellee's preemptory strike of Juror Horace, apparently and correctly denied the appellant's oratory tennis motion for mistrial, and correctly denied the appellant's motion to interview a juror and motion for new trial because of juror misconduct. Those rules were the correct application of applicable and controlling law. And in no instance did the trial court abuse his discretion in this case based upon the foregoing arguments.
